title: 📖 Peoples of the Second Age I — Dwarves, Elves, Humans, Elder Courts & Trading Folk
rawNotionMarkup: Second Age people-by-people annals, Part I. The following are new specific developments building on the already established broad cultural histories. “Awakening” (Years 1–321), “Wonder” (Years 322–1,321) and “Fire” (Years 1,322–1,437) are Avarran labels and year conversions only, not names every continent used. Ancient anecdotes are subject to imperfect Second Age documentary survival; no genuine First Age records exist. Species do not imply one destiny, one temperament, or fixed rates of childbirth. ## Khazari — the stone that tells the truth Years 1–321: After some inherited lunar workings turned unpredictable, a workshop circle in the old Ironspine, the Underbeam Fellowship, refused to let new crews enter an untested load-bearing cavern. Wealthy owners threatened to blacklist its apprentices. When a brace fractured during a storm, workers who had laid an ordinary escape path saved a trapped group, including a foreman who had called them cowards. The incident helped shape the older Two-Hand Rule tradition: every important enchanted structure should have a physical means of inspection and fallback. Yet the debate remained genuine; some runesmiths feared safety inspection would become an excuse to suppress innovation. Years 322–1,321: Competitive runesmith houses and stoneworkers tested new lunar powers against independent masonry. the Kettle-Hammer Trial was a remembered case in which a famous enchanted forge passed ceremonial tests but injured laborers because ordinary ventilation was neglected. Maerin Copper-Tally, a worker and adoptive parent, pressed guild judges to compensate not only master smiths but apprentices, cooks and exhausted haulers. She won compensation in one guild circuit. Another guild never accepted the ruling. Khazari society could honor a childless master, a craftworker with many children, an ordinary parent and an industrious elder; the duty was to contribute, not to achieve one uniform family model. Their modern Seven Thrones and First Throne's precise date are not established here. Years 1,322–1,437: The later Hearth-Gate Agreements of the Era of Fire advanced these arguments without making every older workshop part of a future Throne. ## Eldar — memory, privilege and living roots Years 1–321: Eldar grove keepers studied sky, water, trees and animal cycles when old moon-supported predictions proved unreliable. Their Living Calendar grew from comparing observations by many witnesses. At the Red Leaf Hearing, a noble steward was accused of denying independent farmers access to a needed medicinal grove. A younger healer, Elaneth Thorn-Voice, publicly admitted the grove's previous moon-based timetable had failed and released new harvesting dates. Elders split over whether this courage was admirable or treason to their stewardship. Years 322–1,321: New lunar-derived arts made sophisticated living halls, healing and illumination possible, but also widened the power of those who controlled land and teaching. Several schools formed the Circles of Shared Seed; students carried lessons to farmers and other peoples, while restrictive courts branded them reckless. A court musician, Sorelin Dusk-Note, composed a memorial sung in multiple traditions for workers killed in a magical garden's collapse. Some court elites protested that naming poor dead alongside nobles diminished the institution. The work survived through ordinary public singing. Eldar lifespans gave some individuals direct memory of more than one cultural period, but no living witness or court possessed infallible First Age historical evidence. Years 1,322–1,437: The later regional Grove-Court of Seralith extended the tension between private stewardship and public healing. It is not retroactively the same as every earlier Eldar court or the current High Sovereignty. ## Humans — many kingdoms, no one ancestry Years 1–321: Diverse human river, forest, coastal and grassland societies developed mundane food stores, engineering, medicine and the practical Second Measure: compare what a spell promises with what actually happens. the Broken Bell Petition in one river market protested a governor's decision to pay enchanted advisors while dismissing manual flood workers; the protest won reinstatement of some workers and cost others their freedom. Separate human seafaring communities faced quite different dangers and did not have a single shared ruler. Years 322–1,321: New schools, river leagues, scholarly patronages, harsh tax states and ambitious maritime republics arose in different places. Princess Liora of the Two Marshes commissioned ordinary millworks and public schooling alongside magical irrigation, but also taxed neighboring villages without representation. Her opponents established an independent public measure house; her successor later incorporated parts of its law. Stories remembered her as either a builder or an oppressor depending on who suffered the taxes. No modern Aldermere, Valtoria, Northern Holds, merchant republic or Southern Sultanate is given a mandatory origin through her. Years 1,322–1,437: Regional human histories now include Avarra's Crown of Three Fords and Queen Merea, Sahrad's Blue-Jar Crown, and many other peoples sharing their towns. The global earthquakes ended the Age; no universal human kingdom or species extinction is asserted. ## Drakari — pride beneath an altered sky Years 1–321: True Dragons studied the changed moons in diverse ways. Some offered protection to settlements, some extorted tribute, and some withdrew to isolated territories. Kerev the Copper-Scaled, a dragon whose name appears in separate coast and mountain traditions, argued that powerful beings who charged for protection must also bear a public duty when that protection failed. Others dismissed that as a doctrine for the weak. Neither the accuracy of every legend nor a universal dragon ethic is asserted. A Dragon's longevity is not evidence of an authentic surviving written First Age source. Years 322–1,321: A few independent Drakari courts patronized precise sky observations, metalworking or negotiated sanctuary, while rival individuals hoarded new lunar knowledge. The Dispute of the Ashen Token, preserved in later stories, concerned whether a protection promise could be inherited by a new ruler whose predecessor had died. A dragon arbitrator declined to enforce an unclear contract against a town of strangers, angering the debt-holding lord. The episode should not become an automatic worldwide dragon treaty, established divine revelation or proof that all Drakari loved lesser peoples. Years 1,322–1,437: No blanket Dragon war or creation of Orcs is added to the Era of Fire; individual later roles remain unassigned. ## Aelwyn — promises with teeth Years 1–321: Aelwyn Fae communities encountered changes in lunar-supported rites and safeguards without losing the planet's distinct Natural Magic. A winter dispute remembered as the Gift of Empty Hands involved an Aelwyn court offering refuge for an exchange that neighbors claimed was never clearly explained. A younger court advocate argued that a promise extracted from a hungry child could not be treated like an adult's bargain. The reform applied in one court, not to all Fae or every magically bound agreement. Years 322–1,321: Some seasonal courts designed beautiful hidden estates and subtle healing practices with new lunar workings; others enforced labyrinthine obligations that ruined households. the Moon-Veil Petition was a settlement between one isolated woodland Fae household and its neighboring public town over concealed paths, stray livestock and the right to seek help in a storm. A pair of Fae siblings disagreed fiercely over whether an outsider could freely decline an offered gift. Their argument became a tale taught both as etiquette and as a warning about soft forms of coercion. Aelwyn are not Pixies or Brownies, and their exact moon affinities are not determined. Years 1,322–1,437: Vaelora's regional orchard controversies belong to later history without forcing all Aelwyn into the same polity. ## Goblins — citizens of the roads and records Years 1–321: Goblin farmers, drovers, mixed-city families, salvage crews and traders navigated broken magical safeguards with material stores and careful accounting. Rivva Brass-Note founded a road-credit practice in which a family could claim food against labor already performed instead of pledging a child's future. Some merchants loved it; wealthy creditors threatened to close their stalls. She was not a ruler of all Goblins and did not create a universal Goblin religion. Years 322–1,321: Several Goblin communities became known for compact enchanted instruments and exact trade appraisal. the Thirty Weights Affair exposed a prestigious Human-Goblin merchant syndicate that falsified enchanted weighing tools, impoverishing small farms. A Goblin investigator, Harel Moss-Coin, helped reveal the fraud alongside a human dockworker. Their joint account entered local trade schools as a lesson that deceit belongs to people and institutions, not a species. Goblins established permanent communities as well as traveling ones; later anti-Goblin stereotypes linked to Orc wars are not to be projected into this Age. Years 1,322–1,437: The later Copper-Thread Caravans and western Avarran wartime histories must be dated independently. No Second Age Goblins fought with Orcs, who did not yet exist. ## Ogres — the size of a home is not the size of a character Years 1–321: Ogre families in scattered uplands, rivers, wetlands and market districts rebuilt crossings and food stores, and some isolated forest-dwellers defended their homes fiercely. A large ferryman, Orvak the Marsh Lantern, charged no fee to travelers fleeing a failed magical bridge but demanded payment from passing nobles he knew had confiscated village seed. Critics called him a bandit; rescued families called him a guardian. Other Ogre bands committed genuine crimes and faced resistance. Neither story defined all Ogres. Years 322–1,321: Some Ogre communities combined physical construction with newly mastered enchantments, supporting bridges, foundries, farming and scholarship. the Bent-Axle Dispute began when city officials blamed Ogre haulers for a dangerous cartway designed incorrectly by a wealthy engineer. An Ogre surveyor, Temma Vale-Bridge, produced measurements that embarrassed the city court. She secured wages owed to injured haulers; the court still refused to replace the entire route. Their normal households included children, ordinary craftspeople, elders and self-chosen solitary living. Years 1,322–1,437: The later working communities and tale of Braghal of the Wide Bridge are separate events. Ogre origins and their possible biological relationship to later Orcs remain unsettled. ## Halflings — bread, land and freedom to leave Years 1–321: Halfling kitchen and seed circles helped neighbors survive failed food-preservation enchantments. the Hearth-Salt Agreement in one agricultural district forbade confiscating emergency seed from a household solely because its magical store failed. Richer farms opposed the rule, and it was not followed in all villages. An itinerant healer, Pemma Underbough, became known for traveling beyond her own people to teach safe food preparation. She later refused to join a guild that would have forbidden her to treat nonmembers. Years 322–1,321: Halfling communities could be settled gardeners, sophisticated merchants, scholars, travelers, soldiers and craftspeople. the Orchard Tenancy Struggle in a lowland district opposed a court's attempt to bind families permanently to magically fertile land. A local judge ruled that debt did not by itself erase freedom of movement; powerful landlords kept resisting, but independent farmers won enforceable rights in a few townships. Happiness in shared meals and family life coexisted with real class conflict. Years 1,322–1,437: The later Avarran displaced-families' hearth claims fit this tradition without requiring each modern Halfling borough to descend from it. ## Gnomes — the apparatus that can be questioned Years 1–321: The Empty Bench custom in some Gnomish schools required makers to demonstrate ordinary physical principles before adding enchantment. At the Copper Cylinder Hearing, an apprentice proved that a supposedly lunar-powered water purifier depended on hidden manual pumps maintained by underpaid workers. The inventor kept much of his prestige, but school apprentices began crediting the workers in public diagrams. Not every Gnome was an engineer, and no mysterious “Impossible Engine” was identified. Years 322–1,321: Gnome scholars pioneered public demonstrations, miniature observatories and tests of newer moon magic. the Glass-Bell Failure injured spectators when a celebrated experimental lantern fractured. A researcher, Elri Dapplewrench, opposed the governing guild's attempt to blame the injured audience for standing too close; she demanded posted hazard limits and paid compensation. The reforms spread through teaching networks without suppressing daring experiments entirely. Gnomish households included gardeners, entertainers, parents, merchants and ordinary workers, not just inventors. Years 1,322–1,437: The later measurement and waterworks traditions build on this history without assigning a creator or date to the still-unexplained Impossible Engine. ## Protected uncertainty The original First Throne civilization, the cause of its Silence Below and Gloin Hammerfeld's ancestry remain completely unresolved. No authentic First Age documents were preserved. The original Ironspine predates the First Age. No Orcs existed during the Second Age, regardless of later Goblin or Ogre lore. No regional ancient state named here is automatically the current kingdom of the same continent.
